Defer-reason: tangential

## Current State

`plugin/bin/lib/hooks/pre-tool-use.js`'s `checkWorktreeRequired` (the `worktree-always` gate) denies a Bash call whose command text contains a `>`/`>>`/`>|`/`&>`/`&>>` redirect-shaped substring, to stop an unguarded write to the main checkout outside a worktree. The matcher appears to be purely textual: it does not distinguish a real shell redirect from a `>` that occurs inside embedded heredoc'd source (JS, in practice) passed to `node`.

Confirmed live during a `/claude-tweaks:dispatch next` Routine firing on 2026-10-23, in a non-worktree main-checkout session: `plugin/skills/dispatch/queue-pull-script.md`'s own documented grouping snippet (run via `bin/node-eval-file.js` with a heredoc) contains the literal line `if (openIds.length > 0) excludedNative.push(...)`. Running that exact documented Bash call was refused with the `worktree-always` denial message, even though the command performs no real redirect — its only file target was a `/tmp/ct-session-*` path, nowhere near the repo. Rewriting the comparison to `if (openIds.length) { ... }` (no literal `> ` text) let the identical logic run with no denial, confirming the trigger is textual, not semantic.

Because `queue-pull-script.md` is read and run verbatim by every `/claude-tweaks:dispatch` firing (and other skills following the same node-eval-file.js heredoc convention), any firing that runs in a non-worktree session and reaches this exact line hits the same false block — a Routine firing has no one to retry it by hand.

## Deliverables

- `checkWorktreeRequired`'s redirect-shaped-substring matcher gains awareness of heredoc boundaries (e.g. ignore `>`-shaped text between a `<<'EOF'`/`<<EOF`-style heredoc opener and its matching closing delimiter), or is otherwise scoped to reject only a `>` that is syntactically a shell redirect (preceded by a file-descriptor-less command boundary, not embedded inside a heredoc body).
- `plugin/skills/_shared/policy-schema-coverage.md`'s worktree-always coverage block documents the heredoc exemption explicitly, so a future matcher change doesn't silently regress it.
- A regression test in the existing `pre-tool-use` hook test suite pins a Bash command containing a heredoc with a `>`-shaped numeric comparison (e.g. `x.length > 0`) as allowed, while a real `>` redirect at the top level of the same command (outside any heredoc) is still denied.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The exact `queue-pull-script.md` grouping snippet (containing `if (openIds.length > 0) ...`) runs without a `worktree-always` denial in a non-worktree session, when its only write target is outside the repo (e.g. under `/tmp`).
2. A Bash command with a real top-level `>` redirect into a repo file (outside any heredoc) is still denied in a non-worktree session — no regression to the gate's actual purpose.
3. `npm test` passes.

## Release Note

Internal hardening: the `worktree-always` write gate no longer mistakes a numeric comparison (`x.length > 0`) inside a heredoc-embedded script for a real shell redirect.

## Technical Approach

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/pre-tool-use.js` — `checkWorktreeRequired`'s redirect-shaped-substring matcher
- `plugin/skills/_shared/policy-schema-coverage.md` — document the heredoc exemption
- `tests/` (existing pre-tool-use hook suite) — new regression cases

Surface: infra

## Overview

Nothing in `run-state.json` says whether the session that owns a run is still alive. `updatedAt` moves on non-owner writes (the exemption stamps in `pre-tool-use.js` write to `ctx.runDir` without an ownership check), and a worktree lock PID belongs to the worktree rather than the run and goes stale on resume. Every cleanup decision that follows in this project (closing dead runs, trimming the SessionStart banner) needs one trustworthy answer to "is this run live, dead, or can't we tell?", and today three modules each answer it their own way.

This record adds that answer and changes no behavior. It does two things. It stamps an additive `owner` block into `run-state.json` wherever ownership is already stamped. It adds a new module, `plugin/bin/lib/run-liveness/`, that turns that block plus the existing probes (worktree lock, last commit time, event recency) into a three-valued verdict from positive evidence. No caller consumes the verdict yet; later records in this project migrate callers onto it (#3977 for dead-run closing and the banner, #3979 for the duplicated definitions) and then delete the old definitions.

**Complexity:** Medium
**Estimated tasks:** 7

## Non-Goals

- No caller consumes `runLiveness` in this record: not reconcile, not the SessionStart banner, not `isDeadRunDir`, not `resume-freshness.js`. Migrating callers is a separate record in this project (#3979).
- No auto-close, no archive change, no banner change.
- `updatedAt` is not repurposed. It stays a write timestamp and nothing new reads it as a liveness signal.
- No change to the nested `claude -p` SessionEnd mis-attribution (#3845); this record only has to be correct in the presence of its false `interrupted`.
- No GitHub state changes and no new policy keys. The 10 minute and 72 hour windows are module constants, tuned only with evidence and never in the fail-open direction.

## Prerequisites

| Spec | Title | Status |
|------|-------|--------|
| #3845 | A nested `claude -p` inside a pipeline session marks the parent's run interrupted at its SessionEnd | in progress; the SessionEnd route below must stay correct under its false `interrupted`, and both records touch `session-end.js`/`context.js` neighbourhoods |

## Current State

- Ownership stamps: `record-worktree` in `plugin/bin/hooks.js` (dispatch table at line 106, handler near line 655), `stampAdHocRunDir` in `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/post-tool-use.js` (line 295), and `stampAdHocRunDirForDenial` in `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/context.js` (line 785). Each calls `writeRunState(runDir, { worktree, status: 'active', sessionId })`.
- `writeRunState` (`context.js` line 729) is a read-modify-write under `acquireRunStateLock` with a shallow `{ ...existing, ...patch, updatedAt }` merge. A nested object in the patch replaces the existing one wholesale.
- Probes to reuse, not copy (each wrapped to return a tagged `positive` / `negative` / `error` result; a wrapper may add a read-only export, such as a raw last-commit timestamp getter in `resume-freshness.js`, without changing that file's behavior): `parseWorktreeList`, `isPidAlive`, `lockVerdict` exported from `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/worktree-reap.js`; `checkResumeFreshness` and `RESUME_FRESHNESS_THRESHOLD_MS` (10 minutes) in `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/resume-freshness.js`; `ownEventRecency(runDir)` in `plugin/bin/lib/reconcile/archive-merged.js` (line 263), which reads owner-attributed events from `events.jsonl` via `readEventLines` in `context.js`.
- The duplicated liveness definitions this module will eventually replace: `isDeadRunDir` in `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/run-dir-resolve.js` (line 89), the `abandoned-interrupted` recency test in `classifyRunDir` (`archive-merged.js` line 1602), the probes in `resume-freshness.js`, and the worktree-lock read in `parentLiveDetail` in `plugin/bin/lib/flow/consolidated-pass.js`.
- `isTrustedOwnedRun(ctx.ownedRun)` in `context.js` (line 752) is the existing owner-versus-`fallback` attribution test; `fallback` attribution is a guess at the newest unowned run and is never this session's own.
- Hooks contract: `docs/hooks.md` (the Ownership section at line 44 is where the owner block is documented).
- Tests: `tests/hooks-run-attribution.test.js` and `tests/hooks-context.test.js` for stamp behavior; `tests/bin-lib/reconcile/archive-merged.test.js` for `ownEventRecency` fixtures; the suite for the new module is new.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Task 0, blocking and first: the empirical premise check. Verify that a hook process receives `CLAUDE_PID` (the Bash tool environment carries `CLAUDE_PID`, observed on 2026-10-22 as the PID of the `claude` process in the `ps` ancestry). Probe it from a real hook invocation, record the raw output, and if hooks do not receive it, implement the parent-chain walk to the `claude` process instead. Task 0's output also fixes (a) the exact rule that identifies the `claude` process in the ancestry (executable basename and which ancestor), (b) how a nested `claude -p` is handled (the owner pid is always the process of the session whose `session_id` the hook received, never an ancestor belonging to another session), and (c) the result when neither source resolves a pid (`owner.pid` is `null`, and the run then has no PID evidence). The owner block records which source supplied the pid in `owner.pidSource` (`env` or `ancestry`). Do not write the owner-block contract text or its tests until this result is in hand (`empirical-premise-check-deliverables.md`).
- [ ] `owner` block written by all three stamp sites: `{ sessionId, host, pid, pidSource, pidStartedAt, heartbeatAt }`, in the same `writeRunState` call that writes `sessionId` (so the owner block always belongs to the session recorded in `sessionId`), with `host` from `os.hostname()`, `pid` the Claude Code process, `pidStartedAt` from `ps -o lstart= -p <pid>` on Unix and `null` where the probe cannot run (Windows, or a sandbox without `ps`), and `heartbeatAt` an ISO timestamp. A stamp never replaces an existing owner block whose `sessionId` differs from the caller's, except when that same call also replaces the run's `sessionId` (an explicit adoption through `record-worktree`). `pid` and `pidStartedAt` are always written together in one call.
- [ ] Heartbeat refresh: the owner's own hooks refresh `owner.heartbeatAt` at most once a minute. Only events attributed to the owner refresh it, never a `fallback` attribution. The refresh runs in the hook dispatcher's common path, so every hook event type with a trusted owned run heartbeats, not only PostToolUse. The re-stamp check (stored `pid` against the current process pid) runs on every owner-attributed event regardless of the heartbeat throttle: a resumed session with the same `sessionId` re-stamps `pid` and `pidStartedAt` together on its first event, and its SessionStart handler does this before it spawns the background reconcile pass, so a resumed run is never judged against its previous process.
- [ ] New `plugin/bin/lib/run-liveness/index.js` exporting `runLiveness(runDir, { now, probes }) -> { verdict: 'live' | 'dead' | 'unknown', evidence: [{ probe, result, detail }] }` (one entry per probe consulted, `result` being `positive`, `negative`, or `error`), with every probe injectable (the house runner seam) and defaults wired to the existing probes listed above.
- [ ] The verdict table and precedence rules (below) implemented, including the legacy route for runs with no owner block.
- [ ] A new test suite for the module with one test per table row, including PID reuse, the legacy route, and the SessionEnd route requiring an owner block, plus a fail-open variant of the module that the tests show going red.
- [ ] `docs/hooks.md` documents the owner block (fields, who writes it, heartbeat cadence, that a missing block means legacy and never an error).

Verdict table the module implements:

| Verdict | Requires |
|---|---|
| `live` | Any one of: the owner PID is alive on this host and its start time matches `pidStartedAt`; `heartbeatAt` is within 10 minutes; a worktree lock on the run's worktree reports an in-use PID (`lockVerdict`); the last commit on the run's worktree is under 10 minutes old (the `resume-freshness.js` probe). |
| `dead` | All `live` probes negative and error-free, plus one of: the owner PID was checked on this host and is gone, or alive with a different start time; or status is `interrupted` with `lastEvent: session-end` and no owner heartbeat since. The SessionEnd route applies only to a run that has an owner block. |
| `dead` (legacy route, runs with no owner block) | No owner-attributed event in `events.jsonl` (`ownEventRecency`) for 72 hours, no in-use lock, and no commit on the worktree for 72 hours. The SessionEnd route alone is never enough for a legacy run, so a false `interrupted` from #3845 cannot kill an idle but live legacy run. |
| `unknown` | Anything else: another host, a probe that errored, a null start time with no SessionEnd, a legacy run short of the 72 hour route. |

Precedence and probe semantics (the table alone does not settle conflicting evidence):

- Every probe is consulted, in the order owner PID, heartbeat, worktree lock, last commit, owner-event recency, so the evidence list is complete and deterministic; there is no short-circuit.
- A `positive` live probe yields `live` even when another probe reported `error` (a live verdict never closes anything). Otherwise any `error` entry yields `unknown`, even when a death witness holds. Otherwise `dead` needs a death witness; with none, the verdict is `unknown`.
- "No owner heartbeat since" the SessionEnd stamp means `owner.heartbeatAt` is earlier than the `ts` of the newest `session-end` event in the run's `events.jsonl` (appended by `session-end.js`); no new run-state field is added. An unreadable `events.jsonl` is an `error`.
- The SessionEnd route is the death witness for the case the PID row cannot judge: the owner PID is alive on this host but `pidStartedAt` is `null`, or `pid` is `null`. When the PID row can judge (gone, mismatched start time, or matching start time), it decides and the SessionEnd route adds nothing.
- The worktree lock and last-commit probes return `negative` with detail `no-worktree` when the run records no worktree or the worktree is gone; absence is not an error, and a missing worktree is never itself a death witness.
- Owner-event recency: an unreadable `events.jsonl` is an `error`; a readable file with no owner-attributed events measures its age from the run id's own timestamp, so a legacy run with zero events still needs 72 hours.
- Heartbeat and PID are separate: a long hook-less stretch (a long tool call) can exceed the 10 minute heartbeat window while the PID row still reports `live`; PID-gone counts as a death witness only together with a stale heartbeat, a negative lock and a negative commit probe.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. After `record-worktree`, `stampAdHocRunDir`, and `stampAdHocRunDirForDenial` each run against a fresh run dir, the written `run-state.json` contains `owner.sessionId`, `owner.host`, `owner.pid`, `owner.pidStartedAt` (a string, or `null` when the probe is injected to fail), and `owner.heartbeatAt`; a test per stamp site asserts every field.
2. Two hook events from the owning session 30 seconds apart leave `owner.heartbeatAt` unchanged after the second; a third event 61 seconds after the first advances it. An event attributed `fallback` never changes `owner.heartbeatAt`. A hook from a different `sessionId` never changes the owner block, and a stamp from a different session over an existing owner block leaves it unchanged.
3. A resumed session (same `sessionId`, new pid) leaves a run-state whose `owner.pid` and `owner.pidStartedAt` match the new process after its first event, written together in one `run-state.json` update, and `runLiveness` then returns `live` through the PID row. The SessionStart handler performs that re-stamp before the background reconcile pass is spawned; a test asserts the order.
4. `runLiveness` returns `live` when the owner PID is alive on this host with a start time equal to `pidStartedAt`. When the PID is gone, and every other probe is a clean negative, it returns `dead`. When the PID is alive but its start time differs from `pidStartedAt` (PID reuse), the PID row does not report `live`, and with every other probe a clean negative the verdict is `dead`.
5. Each remaining `live` probe (heartbeat under 10 minutes, in-use worktree lock, last commit under 10 minutes) alone yields `live`, tested one by one with every other probe negative.
6. A run with an owner block whose PID is alive with `pidStartedAt` `null`, status `interrupted`, `lastEvent: session-end`, and a heartbeat earlier than the newest `session-end` event yields `dead` when every `live` probe is a clean negative; the same run with a heartbeat later than that event yields `live` when it is under 10 minutes old and `unknown` otherwise, never `dead`. A run with no owner block and the same `interrupted` shape yields `unknown`, never `dead`. A run whose PID is alive with a matching start time yields `live` whatever its status.
7. A legacy run (no owner block) yields `dead` only when `ownEventRecency` is older than 72 hours, no in-use lock exists, and the last commit on the worktree is older than 72 hours; at 71 hours of event silence it yields `unknown`.
8. A probe that throws or returns an error result yields `unknown`, for each probe in turn. A different `host`, and a null `pidStartedAt` with no SessionEnd evidence, each yield `unknown`.
9. A fail-open variant of the module (probe error mapped to `dead`) is present in the test file as an injected fault and the probe-error tests fail against it; the evidence is recorded in the PR body.
10. The `CLAUDE_PID` premise result, with the raw probe output, is recorded in the PR body, and the owner block's `pid` source in the code matches it.
11. A `run-state.json` with no `owner` key is read by every existing reader without error and `runLiveness` treats it as legacy; a test pins this.
12. Every verdict carries one evidence entry per probe consulted, each with `result` of `positive`, `negative`, or `error`; a test shows that an erroring probe yields an `error` entry (not `negative`) and verdict `unknown`.
13. Precedence: a fixture with a positive heartbeat and an erroring lock probe yields `live`; a fixture with a death witness and an erroring commit probe yields `unknown`; the evidence list has one entry per probe in the stated order in both.
14. A run recording no worktree yields `negative` (`no-worktree`) from the lock and commit probes, not `error`; a legacy run with a readable, empty `events.jsonl` ages from its run id timestamp (a run id 73 hours old yields `dead` through the legacy route, one 71 hours old yields `unknown`).
15. `owner.pidSource` is `env` or `ancestry`; with neither source available `owner.pid` is `null`, and a run with a `null` pid never yields `dead` through the PID row.
16. `docs/hooks.md` names the owner block's fields (including `pidSource`), the precedence rules, and the legacy rule.

## Release Note

Added a per-run liveness record so claude-tweaks can tell a running session's run from an abandoned one, with no change to how runs behave yet.

## Technical Approach

The owner block is additive to `run-state.json`, which installed builds read over this repo's directories and every consumer project's. Readers treat a missing block as legacy and never as an error; nothing is removed or renamed.

`runLiveness` is a pure function over injected probes. Each probe returns a tagged result (positive, negative, or error) so that an error can never be conflated with a negative. The module composes per the precedence rules above: a positive `live` probe yields `live`; otherwise an `error` yields `unknown`; otherwise `dead` requires every `live` probe to be a clean negative plus a death witness; everything else is `unknown`.

### Data / API Surface

`run-state.json` gains:

```json
"owner": { "sessionId": "string", "host": "os.hostname()", "pid": 90405, "pidSource": "env | ancestry", "pidStartedAt": "string or null", "heartbeatAt": "ISO-8601" }
```

`runLiveness(runDir, { now, probes })` returns `{ verdict: 'live' | 'dead' | 'unknown', evidence: [{ probe, result: 'positive' | 'negative' | 'error', detail }] }`. The structured evidence lets a caller tell a probe error from a clean negative (a resume gate fails closed on an error but not on a clean negative). `probes` overrides any of: `pidAlive`, `pidStartTime`, `lockInUse`, `lastCommitAt`, `ownEventAt`, `hostname`.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/run-liveness/index.js` — new module, `runLiveness` and the legacy/SessionEnd routes
- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/context.js` — `stampAdHocRunDirForDenial`, `writeRunState`, `isTrustedOwnedRun`; the shared owner-block builder and heartbeat helper belong here
- `plugin/bin/hooks.js` — `record-worktree` stamp site
- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/post-tool-use.js` — `stampAdHocRunDir` stamp site
- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/session-start.js` — re-stamp of a resumed session's owner block before the background reconcile spawn
- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/worktree-reap.js` — `parseWorktreeList`, `isPidAlive`, `lockVerdict`, reused behind tagged wrappers
- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/resume-freshness.js` — last-commit-recency probe, reused behind a tagged wrapper (a read-only raw-timestamp export may be added)
- `plugin/bin/lib/reconcile/archive-merged.js` — `ownEventRecency`, reused as-is
- `docs/hooks.md` — owner block documentation
- `tests/run-liveness.test.js` — new suite for the module and its fail-open variant

## Gotchas

- ASSUMPTION — verify at build: hook processes receive `CLAUDE_PID` — via Task 0's probe from a real hook invocation. If they do not, walk the parent chain to the `claude` process; do not fall back to `process.ppid` unverified.
- `writeRunState` merges shallowly: writing `{ owner: { heartbeatAt } }` would erase `sessionId`, `pid`, and the rest. A heartbeat or re-stamp must read the existing `owner` and spread it into the patch.
- Never refresh the heartbeat from a `fallback`-attributed event (`isTrustedOwnedRun`): that attribution is a guess at the newest unowned run and is routinely a sibling session's directory. Refreshing it would keep a dead run looking alive.
- `ps -o lstart=` output is locale- and platform-dependent; store the raw trimmed string and compare for equality only, never parse it into a date.
- A heartbeat write is a hook-path write to a shared file: it must honor the never-break-a-session invariant in `docs/hooks.md` (swallow errors, never throw) and be throttled by reading `owner.heartbeatAt`, not by a new marker file.
- Legacy runs have no heartbeat, so "no heartbeat since the SessionEnd stamp" is always true for them; this is why the SessionEnd route requires an owner block.
- The 10 minute window and the 1 minute throttle are coupled: keep the live window at least ten times the throttle through one shared constant pair and a test asserting the ratio. The window is not a liveness guarantee for a session inside a long tool call; the PID row is the backstop for that gap.
- Residual risk, accepted by the design: on a platform where `pidStartedAt` is `null` (Windows, sandboxes), a nested `claude -p` that falsely marks the parent run `interrupted` (#3845) can make the SessionEnd route report `dead` while the parent is idle for more than 10 minutes. The next owner hook heartbeats the run back to `live`. #3845 removes the false stamp at the source.
- Host equality is `os.hostname()` string equality. A container or sandbox with its own PID namespace and the same hostname can make a live owner look gone, which is why PID-gone is a death witness only together with a stale heartbeat and negative lock and commit probes. Process liveness means the session process exists, not that it still drives this run: one long-lived process can leave several runs `live`, which only costs an extra `leave`.
- This module's table is the authority from the day it lands. The four old definitions are frozen (no edits) until #3979 migrates their callers and deletes them.
- ASSUMPTION — verify at build: SessionStart resolves a resumed session's run by `sessionId` (`ctx.ownedRun`) early enough to re-stamp before it spawns the background reconcile pass (`plugin/bin/lib/hooks/session-start.js`); if it cannot, make the re-stamp the first action of the first hook that can.
- Probe errors resolve to `unknown`, never `dead`. Every new probe wrapper needs a test where it throws.
- Windows and sandboxes: PID and start-time probes degrade to `unknown`; apply the `windows-checkout-test-parity` skill to any new path-matching test.
- Hold the in-progress neighbours in mind: #3845 (`session-end.js`), #3836/#3811/#3736 (`context.js` worktree path comparison), and #3937 (`post-tool-use.js` nested-session writes) edit nearby code.

Origin: build final review of #3880

## Current State

At the Wrap-Up Review Console, ratifying an `sdd-ruling-*` item (`apply`, per `wrap-up/review-console-appendix.md`'s `sdd-ruling-*` bullet) writes its ledger row to `accepted` and files nothing; only `reverse` composes a record proposal (`staged/ledger-record-sdd-ruling-{N}.md`). #3880 added a safe-deferral class that console-auto ratifies at `unattended`: `Defers: yes` with exactly one valid `Defer-reason:` header (including `tangential` and `pre-existing-outside-diff`). That deferred work ends as a terminal `accepted` row, the ledger is deleted once nothing is open, and the work reaches no backlog record. This contradicts CLAUDE.md's "No implicit deferrals" and `_shared/deferral-gate.md`'s premise that a `Defer-reason:` goes with a record. It is not a regression: before #3880 every ratified ruling was dropped the same way. Found by #3880's final whole-branch review (finding I-3). The ratify contract is shared by the single-run console (`review-console.md` step 1 and step 7), the multi-spec console (`flow/multispec-review-console.md`), the interactive Override vocabulary (`review-console-interactive.md`), the on-PR console (`_shared/console-on-pr.md`, `_shared/console-execution.md`, `bin/lib/reconcile/console-execute.js`), and `finish-console`.

## Deliverables

Ratifying a deferral ruling (`Defers: yes`, or any `Defer-reason:` header line, with a valid reason) composes a record proposal via `specShapedBody`, the same way `reverse` does today. Current State is the ruling and the finding it deferred; Deliverables is the deferred work; the record carries the staged file's own `Defer-reason:` value. The proposal routes through the console's record-creation step in the same pass. Once the record exists, the ledger row is written `deferred` with Resolution `ratified → #{n}`; if creation fails or is refused, the row stays `open`.

Ratifying a `Defers: no` ruling (a settled design decision) keeps today's `accepted` write-back unchanged.

Apply the same rule at every console surface that ratifies a ruling: single-run, multi-spec, interactive, on-PR/reconciler execution, and `finish-console`.

Add a conformance test pinning the ratify-files-a-record rule in `wrap-up/review-console-appendix.md` and its code twin, if one exists.

## Acceptance Criteria

Ratifying a `Defers: yes` `sdd-ruling-*` item with a valid `Defer-reason:` produces a backlog record carrying that reason, and the ledger row is `deferred` with the record number.

Ratifying a `Defers: no` ruling still writes the row `accepted` with no record.

A refused or failed record creation leaves the row `open`, never `accepted` or `deferred` without a record number.

`npm test` passes in full.

## Release Note

## Current State

Observed during #3845 (run 2026-10-22T033950-record-3845): `_shared/pr-run-comments.md`'s Post-or-update Find step prescribes `gh pr view {pr-number} --repo {host}/{owner}/{repo} --json comments --jq '.comments[] | select(.body | startswith("<!-- run-comment: {kind} -->")) | select(.authorAssociation == ...) | .id'`. In a worktree-isolated session (the shape every dispatched `pr-first` run is in) the harness refused it twice, as `wd-guard-refusal` / `harness-worktree-isolation` events ("runs gh with the text .comments[] | select(.body |… inside a construct too complex to verify"). The first refusal also tripped on the host-qualified `--repo github.com/...` form, whose `github` token reads as a git invocation. The filesystem facts (`docs/journeys/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/`) read the main checkout's files for the same reason.

Observed on run `2026-10-21T225455-record-3679` (PR #3918): the branch renamed and deleted nothing, yet the plan opened the `references` row with ten `R` candidates that were other runs' archived `work/*-spec.md` files, moved on `main` after the branch point. #3017 introduced `resolveRepoRoot` so a shell sitting in a subdirectory of the checkout still finds `docs/journeys/`; the telemetry path rightly anchors to the main checkout (`resolveTelemetryPath`). The facts call reused the same root, which is the wrong anchor for a linked worktree.

Each finding was filed with a trigger condition describing when it would start to matter. Verified against `origin/main` at shaping time:

**scale-readiness (7 items), all in `plugin/bin/lib/code-health/candidates-scale-readiness.js`** unless noted:
1. A capitalized-receiver `X.find(` matches some in-memory constant lookups with a non-function argument, and a filtered `Model.find` with no `.limit` reads as unbounded. (genuinely-larger)
2. `findMany(args)` with a non-literal argument, a spread-only `{ ...opts }`, or a computed `['take']` key reads as unbounded. (genuinely-larger)
3. A module-scope object literal holding a client in a route file (`module.exports = { db: new PrismaClient() }`) reads as `per-request-db-client`, a shape the criteria fragment's What NOT to flag already names. (genuinely-larger)
4. `unbounded-pool` matches non-DB `Pool` classes (generic-pool, undici, workerpool), because it has no DB-dependency gate. The generator already holds `ctx.deps` for its cache and monitoring checks. (needs-human-decision)
5. `window.fetch(` / `globalThis.fetch(` third-party calls on the request path are not matched, because of the dotted-receiver lookbehind. (needs-human-decision)
6. `isRouteFile` is a pure path predicate, while real route membership also needs a server/data dependency or a `"use server"` directive. This is a naming trap for a future second caller; the definition carries a comment saying so. (needs-human-decision)
7. Nuxt, h3, @trpc/server and Elysia apps with only a framework dependency read as not applicable, because `SERVER_DEPS`/`DATA_DEPS` do not name them. (needs-human-decision)

The judge falls back to holistic severity. (needs-human-decision)

## Deliverables

   - scale-readiness item 4: gate `unbounded-pool` on a declared DB dependency (`ctx.deps` against `DATA_DEPS`).
   - scale-readiness item 3: exclude the module-scope client shape already named in the fragment's What NOT to flag.
2. **Decision items surfaced, not decided unilaterally.** Items 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7 and the criteria-fragment calibration were deferred as genuinely-larger or needs-human-decision. For each, the build either implements a fix with tests or records a one-line won't-fix or keep-deferred ruling with its reason. Every needs-human-decision ruling is staged for the human at the run's Review Console, never auto-applied.
3. Each of the nine promoted digest entry lines in #1426 carries `→ #3903`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `normalizeBranch` given two branch bodies that differ only after a `//` inside a string literal treats them as different, and given bodies that differ only in a real `//` comment treats them as equal. A test pins both, and reverting turns it red.
- The comment stripper lives under `plugin/bin/lib/`, and `tests/helpers/strip-comments.js` re-exports or wraps it, so there is one implementation.
- A project with a `new Pool(` from `generic-pool` (or `undici`/`workerpool`) and no DB dependency produces no `unbounded-pool` candidate, while a `pg` `new Pool(` with no `max` still does. Both are tested.
- A route file whose only DB client is held in a module-scope object literal produces no `per-request-db-client` candidate (tested).
- The closing PR, or the run's Review Console staging, states a disposition for every one of the nine items.
- Each of the nine digest entry lines in #1426 carries `→ #3903`.
- `npm test` passes.

## Release Note

Code-health's scale-readiness and experiment-cleanup screens raise fewer false candidates for non-database pools, module-scope clients and comment-like text inside strings.

## Technical Approach

Treat this as three independent slices: the stripper promotion plus `normalizeBranch`; the scale-readiness mechanical fixes (items 3 and 4); and the decision items. The decision items need no code unless a ruling chooses to fix. The `code-health-focus-vertical` and `bin-source-scan-conformance` project skills govern generator anatomy and the shared comment stripper's contract (including its stripper-verdict check), so read both before moving the stripper. Real-input fixtures matter more than synthetic ones for generator changes. Use a fixture that reproduces each false positive rather than a hand-built minimal string.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/code-health/candidates-experiment-cleanup.js` — `normalizeBranch`
- `tests/helpers/strip-comments.js` — the #3585 stripper, to be promoted

## Gotchas

- `tests/helpers/strip-comments.js` is imported by the source-scan conformance suites. Moving it must keep every existing import path working, or the conformance suites lose their stripper silently.
- Five of the nine items were deferred as needs-human-decision. A headless build must stage those rulings rather than settle them; only the three mechanical fixes are unambiguous.

Surface: infra

Origin: reflect full from #3783
**Related:** #205, #3783, #3740, #3508, #3706, #3721, #3905, #3936, #3946, #3963, #3973, #3974, #3975, #3976, #3977, #3979, #3982

## Current State

`plugin/skills/wrap-up/verification-brief-parent-gate.md` treats `$CLOSING_SUB_ISSUES` (the sub-issues a run is closing, which the parent gate counts as `CLOSED` while they are still open) as a prose contract. A table (around line 195) tells each sub-issue-side caller what to pass:

| Caller | Set it passes |
|---|---|
| wrap-up Phase 4 execution | the one sub-issue this run is closing |
| wrap-up auto-merge short-circuit | the one sub-issue this run is closing |
| dispatch group auto-merge gate (`settle-and-merge.md`) | every member of the group (the merge carries one `Fixes #{issue}` per record) |
| dispatch close-out step 3 (`close-out.md:77`) | the PR's `Fixes` record numbers |

Ruling #205 kept this as prose while three callers existed and set "a fourth sub-issue-side caller" as the revisit condition. #3783 (PR #3869) added the fourth (close-out step 3), and the file now defers the decision to this record. An omitted set defaults to `{the sub-issue in hand}`, so the silent-no-op mode is closed, but nothing checks a wrong non-empty set: a caller that passes the wrong records labels the wrong parent's gate.

Every row is a different description of one fact: the records the merge closes. Under `pr-first` that is the PR's `Fixes` lines, which GitHub reports as the PR's `closingIssuesReferences`. `plugin/bin/lib/reconcile/archive-merged.js` already reads that field (around line 320). Under `local-merge`/`current-branch` it is the wrap-up pack's `inputs.closingRecords` (`plugin/bin/lib/wrap-up/pack.js`'s `closingRecords`), the same set the carrier commit's `Fixes` lines are composed from.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Ruling recorded in `verification-brief-parent-gate.md`: `$CLOSING_SUB_ISSUES` is **derived, not passed**. A shared helper computes it from the merge's own closing references, and the per-caller table becomes a description of that derivation.
- [ ] A `plugin/bin/` CLI (e.g. `closing-set.js`) returns the set as JSON: `--pr {n}` reads the PR's `closingIssuesReferences` (reusing `archive-merged.js`'s fetch shape); `--run {dir}` reads `wrap-up-pack.json`'s `inputs.closingRecords` for a run with no PR. An unreadable source exits non-zero with a reason and never prints `[]` as if nothing closes.
- [ ] All four callers call it instead of composing the set by hand: wrap-up Phase 4 execution (`execution-and-verification.md`), the auto-merge short-circuit (`auto-merge-short-circuit.md`), dispatch's group gate (`settle-and-merge.md`), and dispatch close-out step 3 (`close-out.md`)
- [ ] On a helper failure, keep today's default of `{the sub-issue in hand}`, and log the failure so the degraded set is visible
- [ ] A gh-absent (MCP transport) path, per `.claude/skills/mcp-agent-fetch-node-compute`: the agent fetches the PR's closing references through MCP and the helper reads them from a JSON file

## Acceptance Criteria

- Unit tests: a PR whose body closes `#1` and `#2` yields `[1, 2]`; a `--run` dir whose pack lists `[7]` yields `[7]`; a failed PR read and a missing pack each exit non-zero with a reason and print no set
- A conformance test asserts each of the four caller files invokes the helper and none composes `$CLOSING_SUB_ISSUES` by hand
- `verification-brief-parent-gate.md` carries the new ruling, keeps the `{the sub-issue in hand}` default as the failure fallback, and no longer defers to this record
- `npm test` passes

## Release Note

Parent acceptance gates compute which sub-issues a merge closes the same way at every merge site.

## Technical Approach

The original question was a helper versus prose with a new revisit condition. The trade-off it named, a helper "adds a code path every caller threads through" while "prose leaves a wrong non-empty set uncaught", only favors prose if the helper merely takes what the caller hands it. A helper that **derives** the set from the merge's own closing references removes the wrong-value risk entirely: the set equals what GitHub (or the carrier commit) will close, which is the definition the table was approximating. That is what makes the threading cost worth paying, and it also covers a fifth caller by construction instead of by a table row it might misread.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/closing-set.js` — new CLI
- `plugin/bin/lib/wrap-up/closing-set.js` (or a sibling module) — derivation with an injectable runner
- `plugin/bin/lib/reconcile/archive-merged.js` — existing `closingIssuesReferences` read to reuse or extract
- `plugin/bin/lib/wrap-up/pack.js` — `closingRecords` (local-merge source)
- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/verification-brief-parent-gate.md` — ruling and table
- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/execution-and-verification.md` — Acceptance labeling bullet

Surface: infra

Origin: reflect hindsight from #3809
**Related:** #3973, #3736, #3744, #3822, #3876, #3900, #3915, #3974, #3975, #3978, #3979, #3983, #3989

## Current State

`plugin/skills/flow/worktree-merge.md` step 5's **Resolve now** bullet (line 127) carries a multi-run chase. A conflict resolution during a multi-run `local-merge` reconciliation ends in a `git commit`, and E1 (`runInner`'s tail loop in `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/pre-tool-use.js`) checks every commit against `ctx.runDir`, the newest non-terminal run in the project regardless of owner (`docs/hooks.md`'s "Two resolutions, not one"). The main checkout (or, under `worktree-always`, the scratch worktree the resolution runs in) is not any run's assigned worktree, so E1 denies unless the caller's ownership classifies as `foreign`, and the reconciling session usually owns the sibling runs. The procedure therefore closes this branch's run, then each other reconciliation branch's run E1 names in turn, and re-protects each one when the resolution lands or is abandoned.

That bullet drew #3809's whole-branch review Important 1, part of fix round 1, and four `/review` findings (3c at `:126` reproduced, plus single-agent 3b `:126`, 3c `:139`, 3f `:138`). The prose is correct today but is the most fragile part of the procedure, and it exists only because E1 cannot tell that a commit is concluding a merge of a live run's branch. E1's own deny message already names that case as legitimate ("If this checkout is intentionally correct (e.g. finishing the branch), clear the assignment first").

## Deliverables

- [ ] Add a live-query exemption to E1, of the same shape as `isIntegrationBranchFastForwardPush` (#2542): a `commit` target is allowed when its checkout has a merge in progress (a `MERGE_HEAD` exists) **and** every commit `MERGE_HEAD` lists equals the current `HEAD` of a live run's worktree (`ctx.runState.worktree` or any entry in E1's existing `otherWorktrees` map). Log a new `wd-merge-finish` event (expected, actual, merged run dir) to `ctx.runDir` and allow.
- [ ] Every unprovable answer keeps today's E1 verdict (no exemption): no readable `MERGE_HEAD`, a `MERGE_HEAD` commit matching no live run's worktree `HEAD`, a run worktree whose `HEAD` cannot be read (removed worktree, git failure, timeout), or a target action other than `commit`
- [ ] Simplify `worktree-merge.md` step 5's Resolve-now bullet: drop the E1 chase (closing and re-protecting other reconciliation branches' runs) and keep the per-branch close-run ordering #3809 pinned (this branch's run closed first, re-protected after a step 4 failure)
- [ ] Document the exemption in `docs/hooks.md` beside E1's posture bullets

## Acceptance Criteria

- In `tests/hooks-pre-tool-use.test.js`, a `git commit` in a checkout whose `MERGE_HEAD` equals a live sibling run's worktree `HEAD` is allowed and logs `wd-merge-finish`, while `ctx.runDir` names a different (newer) run
- The same commit is still denied when `MERGE_HEAD` is absent, when it names a commit that is no live run's worktree `HEAD`, when one of several `MERGE_HEAD` lines matches no live run, and when the matching run's worktree `HEAD` cannot be read. Each is its own test case.
- A `git push` or non-commit action is unaffected by the exemption
- Each new allow test goes red when the exemption is reverted (`git checkout --` on `pre-tool-use.js` only)
- `worktree-merge.md`'s Resolve-now bullet no longer instructs closing or re-protecting other branches' runs, and the existing #3809 ordering pins still pass
- `npm test` passes

## Release Note

Resolving a merge conflict during a multi-run local-merge reconciliation no longer has to close other branches' runs first.

## Technical Approach

The decision between the three signals the original request listed:

- **A run-state marker set and cleared by the reconciliation** was rejected. It adds a lifecycle (set before the merge, cleared on land or abandon) that the chase itself shows is fragile, and a marker left behind by a crash is a standing allow for that run's commits in the wrong checkout.
- **Narrowing E1's owner-unfiltered newest-run resolution in the main checkout** was rejected. The reconciling session usually owns the runs it merges, so their ownership verdict is `'mine'` and E1 would still deny. Narrowing further would also loosen E1 for the wrong-checkout commit it exists to catch.
- **A `MERGE_HEAD`-keyed live query** was chosen. Git already records the fact E1 lacks: a merge commit in progress whose parent-to-be is a live run's branch tip is that branch being integrated, not that run's work landing in the wrong checkout. It needs no new state, cannot go stale (git removes `MERGE_HEAD` when the merge concludes or aborts), and covers the `worktree-always` path too, where the resolution commits inside a scratch worktree that no run is assigned to.

Implementation follows `.claude/skills/pre-tool-use-gate-exemptions`: read `MERGE_HEAD` via `git rev-parse --git-path MERGE_HEAD` in the target's toplevel (a linked worktree's git dir differs from the main checkout's), compare commit ids exactly, read each candidate worktree's `HEAD` with `git -C {worktree} rev-parse HEAD`, resolve paths through `canonicalRealpath`, and fail closed on every inconclusive read.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/pre-tool-use.js` — E1 tail loop in `runInner`: the `MERGE_HEAD` live-query exemption and `wd-merge-finish` event
- `plugin/skills/flow/worktree-merge.md` — step 5 Resolve-now bullet: drop the E1 chase
- `docs/hooks.md` — E1 posture bullets
- `tests/hooks-pre-tool-use.test.js` — allow and fail-closed cases
- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/context.js` — `appendEvent` (no change expected)

## Gotchas

- The exemption must sit after the `otherWorktrees` check and before the `foreign`-ownership branch. That way it never reclassifies a commit already allowed as `wd-ambiguous`, and a `foreign` caller keeps its existing allow + `systemMessage`.
- Under `worktree-always`, the fast-forward of the main checkout is `git merge --ff-only`, which is not a `commit` target, so only the scratch-worktree commit needs the exemption. Confirm with `gitTargetsFrom` before assuming otherwise.
- An octopus merge lists several commits in `MERGE_HEAD`; require every line to match, so a merge that also pulls in an unrelated branch keeps today's deny.
- The `worktree-merge.md` bullet is pinned by #3809's conformance tests; keep "this branch's run is closed first" and the step 4 re-protection wording intact.

## Original request

Let E1 allow a multi-run reconciliation's conflict-resolution commit without closing sibling runs

Origin: reflect hindsight from #3809

Defer-reason: tangential

## Current State

`plugin/skills/flow/worktree-merge.md` step 5's **Resolve now** bullet carries a multi-run chase: the conflict resolution ends in a commit in the main checkout, which the working-directory hook (E1, `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/pre-tool-use.js`) checks against the newest non-terminal run in the project regardless of owner (`plugin/bin/hooks.js` resolveRunDir, owner-unfiltered). So before the commit can land, the procedure closes this branch's run, then every other reconciliation branch's run E1 names in turn, and must re-protect each one when the resolution lands or is abandoned.

That one bullet drew #3809's whole-branch review Important 1, part of fix round 1, and four /review findings (3c at :126 reproduced, plus single-agent 3b :126, 3c :139, 3f :138). The prose workaround is correct now but is the most fragile part of the procedure, and it exists only because E1 cannot tell that a main-checkout commit belongs to a human-present reconciliation.

## Deliverables

Decide how E1 should treat a commit in the main checkout made while reconciling several runs' branches — so the reconciliation does not have to close sibling runs to get its resolution commit through — and implement that decision in the hook.

Then simplify `plugin/skills/flow/worktree-merge.md` step 5's Resolve-now bullet to drop the E1 chase, keeping the per-branch close-run ordering #3809 pinned.

## Open Question

Which signal should let E1 allow this commit without closing other runs: a run-state marker that the reconciliation sets (and clears) on each run it is merging, a reconciliation-scoped exemption keyed on MERGE_HEAD naming a branch whose run is in the reconciliation, or narrowing E1's owner-unfiltered newest-run resolution for the main checkout? Each changes the never-break-a-session posture in docs/hooks.md differently.

## Release Note

Resolving a merge conflict during a multi-run local-merge reconciliation no longer has to close other branches' runs first.

## Technical Approach

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/pre-tool-use.js` — E1 decision for a reconciliation commit in the main checkout
- `plugin/skills/flow/worktree-merge.md` — drop step 5's E1 chase

Surface: infra

Origin: ledger resolve gate (#3304 final review, I3)
**Related:** #3304, #3675, #3818, #3820, #3876, #3936

## Current State

`plugin/bin/lib/hooks/harness-refusal.js` defines `REFUSAL_FRAGMENTS` (`This session`, ` is isolated in the worktree `, `Refusing to run it`) and `HARNESS_ISOLATION_REFUSAL_RE`, which require the noun `This session`. `post-tool-use-failure.js` uses the regex to log a `wd-guard-refusal` event, and `bash-prefilter.js` uses the signature. The reflect Friction lens reads those events. `tools/upstream-drift/manifest.yml`'s `claude-code` entry asserts each fragment against the installed binary, and `tests/harness-refusal-drift-pin.test.js` keeps the two in lockstep.

Probed against the installed Claude Code 2.1.302 binary (2026-10-24), the refusal noun is chosen by one function:

```
function NI(e){return Tl()?.worktreePath===e
  ? {noun:"This session",possessive:"a worktree-isolated session's"}
  : {noun:"This agent",possessive:"a worktree-isolated agent's"}}
```

So every refusal template (`${noun} is isolated in the worktree …`) says `This agent` whenever the worktree is not the session's own, which is the case for a subagent dispatched with its own isolation worktree. Two more templates are fixed strings: `This agent is isolated in the worktree … no longer exists and the only recovery target is the parent session's shared checkout. Refusing to run there …` and a `${noun}` variant ending `Refusing to run there. Report this instead of retrying.` Neither the `This agent` noun nor `Refusing to run there` matches today's regex, so those refusals produce no `wd-guard-refusal` event.

Lens agents running inside the parent session's own worktree do say `This session` and were counted. That is how #3480's roughly 14 lens-agent refusals surfaced and led to #3675's dispatch-prompt fix. The same waste from an agent in its own isolation worktree is invisible today.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Count both: widen the matcher to the `This agent` noun and to the worktree-gone `Refusing to run there` ending, keeping the `This session` match unchanged
- [ ] Add two fields to each `wd-guard-refusal` event: `actor` (`session` or `agent`, read from the noun) and `variant` (`guard` for the command-shape and different-worktree refusals, `worktree-gone` for the two "no longer exists" templates), so the Friction lens can report the operator's own friction separately from dispatched agents' and flag lost isolation
- [ ] Update `REFUSAL_FRAGMENTS` and the `claude-code` manifest `must-match` values together (noun alternatives plus the `Refusing to run there` signature), and keep `tests/harness-refusal-drift-pin.test.js` in lockstep
- [ ] Have the reflect Friction lens break the count down by `actor` and call out any `worktree-gone` event by name

## Acceptance Criteria

- `tests/hooks-harness-refusal.test.js` logs a `wd-guard-refusal` event for each of: a `This session … Refusing to run it` refusal (`actor: session`), a `This agent … Refusing to run it` refusal (`actor: agent`), a `This agent … Refusing to run it there` different-worktree refusal, and both worktree-gone templates (`variant: worktree-gone`); and logs none for an unrelated Bash failure
- Reverting the widened regex turns the agent and worktree-gone cases red, while the session case stays green
- `tools/upstream-drift`'s `claude-code` check passes against 2.1.302 with the new `must-match` values, and the drift-pin test passes
- `bash-prefilter.js`'s signature check still fires on every matched refusal
- `npm test` passes

## Release Note

Reflect's friction report now counts worktree-guard refusals hit by dispatched agents, not just by the main session.

## Technical Approach

The question was whether these refusals are the run operator's friction. They are the run's friction either way. A dispatched agent's refused command is a wasted turn the run pays for, and it is almost always caused by the dispatch prompt the run wrote, which is exactly the signal that produced #3675's fix. Leaving the narrow match would keep that signal for agents sharing the parent's worktree but hide it for agents in their own, an accident of how the agent was dispatched rather than a deliberate scope. The `actor` field keeps "my own friction" answerable without discarding the rest.

Build the regex from fragments as today: a noun alternation (`This session|This agent`), the isolation clause, a lazy gap, then `Refusing to run` followed by ` it` or ` there`. Derive `actor` from the matched noun, and `variant` from the presence of "no longer exists".

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/harness-refusal.js` — fragments, nouns, signature, regex
- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/post-tool-use-failure.js` — event fields `actor` / `variant`
- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/bash-prefilter.js` — signature check derived from the module
- `tools/upstream-drift/manifest.yml` — `claude-code` `must-match` values and their comment block
- `tests/hooks-harness-refusal.test.js` — new matcher cases
- `tests/harness-refusal-drift-pin.test.js` — lockstep pin
- `plugin/skills/reflect/full-mode.md` — the Friction lens's breakdown by `actor` (the file that reads `wd-guard-refusal`)

## Gotchas

- `harness-refusal.js` must still require nothing (`bash-prefilter.js` loads it on every failed Bash call), so build the widened regex from string constants only.
- The manifest's comment records per-version occurrence counts (`noun:"This session"` 1x at 2.1.302, and so on); update the counts with the new fragments, measured against the installed binary, not guessed.
- ASSUMPTION — verify at build: a subagent's failed Bash call fires the parent session's `PostToolUseFailure` hook with the refusal text intact (the #3480 lens-agent events suggest yes for agents in the parent's worktree); confirm the same for an agent dispatched with `isolation: "worktree"` before relying on the new `actor: agent` events appearing.

## Original request

Decide whether friction events should count the subagent and worktree-gone isolation refusals

Origin: ledger resolve gate

Defer-reason: needs-human-decision

## Current State

`HARNESS_ISOLATION_REFUSAL_RE` in `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/harness-refusal.js` matches only the session noun ("This session is isolated in the worktree ... Refusing to run it"). A subagent's refusal ("This agent is isolated in the worktree ...") and the worktree-gone variant (ending "Refusing to run there") are not logged as `wd-guard-refusal`, so the reflect Friction lens never sees them. Found in #3304's final review (I3).

## Deliverables

Make the decision, then either widen `HARNESS_ISOLATION_REFUSAL_RE` and `REFUSAL_FRAGMENTS` (with the manifest must-match values and the pin tests) or record that the narrow match is intended.

## Open Question

Should the Friction lens count a subagent's and a worktree-gone refusal as the run operator's friction? If yes, widen the regex and `REFUSAL_FRAGMENTS` together with the manifest `claude-code` must-match values; if no, record that the narrow match is intended.

## Release Note

No user-visible change.

## Technical Approach

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/harness-refusal.js` — fragments and regex
- `tools/upstream-drift/manifest.yml` — claude-code assertions

Surface: infra

Origin: SDD whole-branch review of #3595 (run 2026-10-20T124821-spec-3599-3602-3695-3696-3698-3699-3595), finding 2
**Related:** #3812, #3942, #2713, #3396, #3467, #3646, #3721, #3744, #3754, #3843, #3847, #3877, #3878, #3900, #3901, #3902, #3903, #3904, #3968, #3976

## Current State

Under `integration-model: pr-first`, wrap-up's branch-finish merge runs at `review-console.md`'s "On approval" step 13 (#3595): after the console's step-12 commit and a push, before step 14 hands off to Phase 4's execution step (`execution-and-verification.md`). Everything the execution step changes in the tree therefore lands after `gh pr merge`, on a branch that is already merged, and its "Phase exit" push targets that merged branch. Nothing checks that a commit made after the merge is empty (`_shared/pr-first-merge.md` Step 1.5 guards only curation-engine commits).

Inventory of the execution step's actions on `origin/main`, classified against the console's steps 1-13 (`review-console.md`, `review-console-appendix.md`'s Resolution-to-step mapping, `cleanup-procedures.md`'s canonical list):

| Action | Changes tracked files? | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| Reference repairs (staged, approved) | yes | **post-merge residue** — the mapping says a Reference repairs row "has no numbered step of its own — it is applied by Phase 4's execution step" |
| Genre convention resolution | yes — `.claude-tweaks/policy.yml` write, plus `git mv` and reference rewrites on migration | **post-merge residue** — no console step applies it |
| Cleanup item 3 (design caches) | yes — deletes `docs/plans/*-audit.json`/`-recommendations.json`/`-declined.json` (not gitignored) | **post-merge residue** |
| Cleanup item 1 (plans) | yes, under `superpowers-plans-retention: prune-after-wrapup`, and for any leftover `*-design.md` | **post-merge residue** (conditional) |
| Cleanup item 5 (record lifecycle) | yes under `work-backend: local-files` (`closeRecord` + commit); no-op under `github-issues` | **post-merge residue** (conditional) |
| Execution step's own commit + phase-exit push | carries all of the above | **post-merge residue** |
| Documentation, CLAUDE.md/rules, ADRs, new docs (D2), skill updates | yes | **already applied** by console steps 2-5; the execution step's apply list re-lists them |
| Docs-health restructural filings (D1) | no (GitHub issues) | **already applied** by console step 3 — a second pass risks a duplicate `gh issue create` |
| Memory, upstream feedback | no | already confirm-only |
| Acceptance labeling | no (labels, comments) | not tree-changing |
| Cleanup items 2, 4, 6, 7, 8 | no / already routed | item 2 already runs at step 13; item 4's merge is step 13; 6/7 are not tree changes; item 8's run dir is gitignored |

Under "Approve all, leave PR open" no merge runs, so the execution step's commit and push are correct there today — only the merge path is wrong.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Make `pr-first`'s branch finish run once, **after the last tree-changing action of the wrap-up** and before cleanup item 4's worktree removal, instead of at console step 13. Every residue row in the table then reaches the PR head before `gh pr merge`, and the execution step's commit and phase-exit push target a live branch. Item 2's delete-ledger keeps its "after the ledger's last writers, before the merge" placement.
- [ ] The finish still runs when the execution step is skipped ("No actions to execute") and when the console is skipped (empty-console fast path) — one finish point reached on every path, never zero or two
- [ ] Under `pr-first`, the execution step's apply-list entries that console steps 2-5 already applied (Documentation, CLAUDE.md/rules, ADRs, new docs, skill updates, docs-health filings) become confirm-only, the way Memory and Upstream feedback already are — no second application and no second `gh issue create`
- [ ] Update every citation of "step 13" as the merge point: `cleanup-procedures.md`'s Item 2 paragraph, `cleanup-procedures-execution.md` Section C, `merge-mode.md` step 1, and the `auto-merge-short-circuit.md` / `flow/multispec-review-console.md` ordering notes that cite it
- [ ] `local-merge` and `current-branch` behavior is unchanged

## Acceptance Criteria

- A conformance test pins that, under `pr-first`, no tree-changing action in `execution-and-verification.md` or cleanup items 1, 3, and 5 is ordered after the branch-finish merge; reverting the reorder turns it red
- The same test (or a sibling) pins that the execution step's apply list marks the console-applied entries confirm-only under `pr-first`
- A `pr-first` "Approve all + merge" run with a design-wrapper cache or an approved reference repair produces a squash commit containing that change, and no commit lands on the branch after the merge — checked against a real run before and after the fix, quoting the PR's commit list
- "Approve all, leave PR open" still pushes the execution step's commit to the open PR
- `npm test` passes

## Release Note

Wrap-up's final cleanup and commit now land in the merged PR instead of on an already-merged branch.

## Technical Approach

The root cause is the merge's position, not any one action, so the fix moves the merge rather than chasing each residue item into the console. Adding console steps for reference repairs, genre conventions, and cleanup items 1/3/5 would fix today's inventory, but every future execution-step action would reopen the gap. With one finish point after the last tree writer, new actions are covered by default.

Suggested shape (the builder may choose another that meets the constraints): console steps 1-12 unchanged; step 13 becomes "item 2 + push" only (or folds into the execution step); the execution step runs its tree-changing work, commits, and pushes; then a single Branch finish step runs `_shared/pr-first-merge.md` (or leave-open), then cleanup items 4, 6, 7, 8. When the execution step is skipped, the Branch finish step still runs straight after the console.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/review-console.md` — "On approval" steps 13-14
- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/execution-and-verification.md` — apply list (confirm-only under `pr-first`), commit, phase-exit push, leave-open re-check
- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/cleanup-procedures.md` — Item 2 paragraph, canonical order
- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/cleanup-procedures-execution.md` — Section C (merge already routed)
- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/merge-mode.md` — step 1 cites step 13
- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/SKILL.md` — Phase 4's "No actions to execute" skip and the empty-console fast path
- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/review-console-appendix.md` — Resolution-to-step mapping (Reference repairs row)
- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/auto-merge-short-circuit.md` — ordering note

Surface: infra

Origin: reflect (light mode, Friction lens) from #3675's wrap-up run (2026-10-20T162315-record-3675).
**Related:** #3690 (absorbed), #3188, #3295, #3737, #3740, #3812, #3898, #3956, #3963

## Current State

In #3675's dispatch group, both dispatched Task calls — `build,test` and `review,polish,wrap-up` — found mid-run that no `Agent`/`Task` tool was available, ran their work inline, and each self-reported the gap in `decisions.md` as a `DONE_WITH_CONCERNS` deviation. Nothing defective shipped, but the same discovery happened twice in one run.

Since then, half of this is settled. #3078 (`364762254`) gave `_shared/subagent-dispatch-core.md`'s Foreground Execution Discipline a **Fallback** for "no `Agent`/`Task` tool exists (`ToolSearch` finds none, deferred or otherwise — the normal case in a cloud routine sandbox)", restated in `dispatch/task-prompt.md`'s Context pack item 7: judge the unit in-session, log the downgrade, mark its findings `unconfirmed`. That covers read-only units (lenses, single reads, judges) — the review call's side.

The build side is still uncovered, and two rules now contradict each other there:

- The Fallback is explicitly limited to read-only units; for a write-capable child it says only that one still silent at the bound is never redone in-session (because an abandoned child keeps running and may still write).
- `build/execution-mode-policy.md` (#491) rules that executing the plan's substance directly in-session, skipping Task dispatch, is **never licensed** — under a locked `execution-strategy: subagent-only` or otherwise.

The same environment has already produced two different outcomes. In run `2026-10-20T022848-record-3630` (record #3630, filed as #3690, absorbed here), the dispatched build stopped at `/build`'s Common Step 2 before any implementation (#3690's report calls it a HARD-GATE; `build/SKILL.md` has no gate by that literal name there, so the stop presumably came from the call honoring `execution-mode-policy.md`'s never-licensed rule), and Settle classified it `transient` and kept `auto:build`, so every retry in that sandbox would stop the same way. In #3675's run, the build ran inline instead and reported a concern.

So a dispatched `build,test` call under `execution-strategy: subagent-only` that has no `Agent` tool has no compliant path: `/superpowers:subagent-driven-development` cannot dispatch implementers, inline execution is forbidden, and nothing says to stop. #3675's call improvised inline execution and reported it as a concern. Nothing about this case is anomalous — the core file itself calls it the normal case in a cloud routine sandbox — yet each call discovers it mid-run, after the plan is written.

## Deliverables

- [ ] `_shared/subagent-dispatch-core.md`'s Foreground Execution Discipline names the **no-nested-agent environment** once, as an expected environment class, and distinguishes its two cases: a child abandoned at the bound (today's rule — a write-capable one is never redone in-session) versus a child that was **never launched because no `Agent` tool exists** (no child exists, so nothing can still be writing, and the unit — write-capable or not — is done in-session)
- [ ] `build/execution-mode-policy.md` gains one carve-out to #491's "never licensed": a dispatched Task call (not the interactive orchestrating session) that has no `Agent` tool executes the plan in-session. State why this keeps #491's rationale: the dispatched call is already a clean room separate from the session that dispatched it, and the second Task call (`review,polish,wrap-up`) remains a separate agent, so the review is still independent of the code's author
- [ ] `dispatch/task-prompt.md`'s first-call (`build,test`) template tells the call to probe for the `Agent` tool once, **before** choosing an execution strategy (one `ToolSearch`), and on no tool to take the carve-out from the start instead of discovering it mid-plan; Context pack item 7 carries the same distinction for any dispatch that writes
- [ ] The downgrade logs as one canonical `decisions.md` `AUTO` entry (per `_shared/auto-decision-log.md`'s schema) naming the environment — e.g. `no nested Agent tool — plan executed in-session` — and the call returns `STATUS: DONE`, not `DONE_WITH_CONCERNS`, when that was the only deviation
- [ ] The read-only Fallback keeps its `unconfirmed` marking unchanged — a self-judged lens finding is still weaker evidence than a second reader's

## Acceptance Criteria

- `subagent-dispatch-core.md` states that a write-capable unit whose child was never launched (no `Agent` tool) is executed in-session, and that a write-capable child abandoned at the bound still ends `STATUS: BLOCKED` — both rules present, and distinguishable by whether a child was ever launched
- `build/execution-mode-policy.md` names the dispatched-call-with-no-`Agent`-tool carve-out and still states that the interactive orchestrating session may never execute the plan directly
- `dispatch/task-prompt.md`'s `build,test` template contains the up-front probe instruction, ordered before the execution-strategy choice
- `tests/foreground-execution-instruction.test.js` (or the suite that pins these sections) asserts the new never-launched-vs-abandoned distinction in the core section, item 7, and the build template, and reverting the core-file sentence turns it red
- The canonical `AUTO` line's wording is pinned in one place and cited, not restated, by the template
- A `/claude-tweaks:dispatch` firing against a `subagent-only` record, in an environment whose dispatched Task call has no `Agent` tool, builds via the carve-out rather than stopping at Common Step 2 or being settled `transient` (the #3690 failure)
- `npm test` passes

## Release Note

Dispatched builds in sandboxes without nested agents now follow a defined path instead of improvising and flagging a concern.

## Technical Approach

The key distinction is whether a child was ever launched. The existing "never redo a write-capable child in-session" rule exists because an abandoned child keeps running and may still write (`subagent-dispatch-core.md`'s Fallback). With no `Agent` tool there is no child, so that hazard cannot occur, and in-session execution of a write-capable unit is safe. Write that reasoning into the core file once, and have `task-prompt.md` item 7 and the `build,test` template restate the rule (they are inlined verbatim into a `Task()` prompt whose agent never reads the core file — `docs/skill-graph.md`'s `subagent-dispatch-core.md` row).

The probe is one `ToolSearch` for the `Agent` tool at the start of the `build,test` call. A probe by the top-level dispatcher would not work: the dispatcher has a Task tool by construction (it is dispatching), and whether its children get a nested one depends on the environment and Claude Code version (`subagent-dispatch-core.md`'s Background-work paragraph, #3722's measurements).

#491's carve-out is narrow on purpose: it licenses in-session execution only for a dispatched Task call that has no `Agent` tool. An interactive session that has the tool and chooses not to use it is still non-compliant.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-dispatch-core.md` — Foreground Execution Discipline: name the environment class; never-launched vs abandoned
- `plugin/skills/build/execution-mode-policy.md` — the dispatched-call carve-out to #491
- `plugin/skills/dispatch/task-prompt.md` — Context pack item 7 and the `build,test` template's up-front probe
- `plugin/skills/_shared/auto-decision-log.md` — only if the canonical entry needs a new reason slug
- `tests/foreground-execution-instruction.test.js` — pins the core section, item 7, and both templates
- `tests/subagent-contract-clauses.test.js` — check for pinned Fallback wording
- `docs/skill-graph.md` — the `subagent-dispatch-core.md` edge row describing what item 7 restates

## Gotchas

- `/flow`'s `multispec-parallel-waves.md` inlines item 7 and the `build,test` clause verbatim (`docs/skill-graph.md`), so changing either changes what parallel-wave members receive — update that file in the same change.
- `tests/foreground-execution-instruction.test.js` pins the core section, item 7, and both templates against each other; edit all four together or it goes red.
- The decision is about the dispatched Task call, not `/superpowers:subagent-driven-development` itself (an upstream skill this repo does not edit) — the carve-out tells the call to execute the plan in-session in place of invoking that skill.
- #3188 (open) proposes mechanical enforcement of `execution-strategy: subagent-only` (a PreToolUse check or a `/build` Step 2 assertion). Whatever it lands must honor this carve-out — a dispatched call with no `Agent` tool executing in-session is compliant, not a violation.
- `/build`'s Common Step 2 is where #3630's build stopped; the carve-out has to be reachable from there (the probe result decides the execution strategy before Common Step 2 resolves it), or the build stops anyway.
- ASSUMPTION — verify at build: #3675's two calls lacked the tool because of the environment (cloud sandbox or a headless Claude Code version), not a one-off harness fault — the run's `decisions.md` was not preserved in the archive, so confirm the class by checking `subagent-dispatch-core.md`'s Background-work measurements against the run's environment if it can be identified.

## Original request

Dispatch contract doesn't name or detect an Agent/Task-tool-less sandbox

Origin: reflect (light mode, Friction lens) from #3675's wrap-up run (2026-10-20T162315-record-3675).
Defer-reason: tangential

## Current State

`_shared/subagent-dispatch-core.md`'s subagent contract, and `dispatch/settle-and-merge.md`'s
two-call gate, assume `execution-strategy: subagent-only` dispatched Task calls have the
Agent/Task tool available for nested fan-out. In this run's dispatch group (record #3675), both
dispatched calls — `build,test` and `review,polish,wrap-up` — independently discovered mid-run
that no Agent/Task tool was available, and both fell back to running their work inline, each
self-reporting the gap in `decisions.md` as a `DONE_WITH_CONCERNS` deviation. Both degraded
gracefully and no defect landed in the shipped work, but the gap recurred identically across two
independent calls in the same run rather than being a one-off anomaly.

## Open Question

Should the dispatch contract (or dispatch's own two-call gate) detect Agent/Task-tool absence up
front — either declaring the limitation inline in the dispatch prompt's own preamble, or treating
a Task-tool-less sandbox as a named, expected environment class — rather than leaving each
dispatched call to discover and self-report the gap independently every time? Or is the existing
per-call self-report-and-degrade pattern (DONE_WITH_CONCERNS + a decisions.md note) sufficient as
is, given it already surfaces the gap without blocking?

## Release Note

n/a — no code change proposed yet; this issue exists to get a maintainer decision on whether one
is warranted.

Surface: infra

Origin: ledger resolve gate (wrap-up of #3664, ledger rows 3-4)
**Related:** #3664, #3646, #3792, #3942

## Current State

The ephemeral dev server a pipeline starts (`_shared/dev-url-detection.md`'s Ephemeral server start, items 3-4) is recorded as one line, `{pid} {port} {worktree-root} detached:{yes|no}`, in `ephemeral-server.txt`. POSIX launches under `setsid` and records `detached:yes`; Windows has no detach primitive and records `detached:no` (`dev-url-detection.md:130-131`). The recorded pid is the shell leader; the listening socket can belong to its child.

Every stop identifies the server only by that pid and port. `wrap-up/cleanup-procedures-execution.md` Section D (#3664) validates the record's shape and keeps it when the port is still held after the kill, but proves neither identity:

- **Kill side (step 2):** any positive-integer pid is signalled (`kill {pid}`, plus `kill -- -{pid}` under `detached:yes`; `taskkill /PID {pid} /T /F` on win32). A pid reused by an unrelated process after the server died gets killed, along with its tree on win32.
- **Port side (step 4):** a port still held after an "already stopped" pid is reported as the server's survivor, though the holder may be an unrelated process.

A "pid listens on port" probe does not settle it, because the listener is usually the leader's child, and after the leader dies a non-detached child is reparented, so a parent-chain walk breaks.

The same stop logic is restated as agent-read prose in other places: `review/step3-routing.md`'s fix-wave server coordination (around line 124), `_shared/dev-url-detection.md`'s standalone stop, `flow/multispec-review-console.md`'s shared teardown (line 176), and `flow/multispec-parallel-waves.md`'s per-member stop (line 54). Each guard is pinned by text, not by behavior.

## Deliverables

- [ ] **Identity rule:** a process is identified by `(pid, start time)`. When the server starts, capture two identities: the **leader** (the pid recorded today) and the **listener** (the process holding the port once the readiness poll in item 3 succeeds). Write both, with start times, to a sidecar `ephemeral-server.json` beside `ephemeral-server.txt`. The txt line keeps its format, since `detached:` is parsed as its last token.
- [ ] **Kill side:** signal a recorded process only when its current start time matches the recorded one; a mismatch or a missing pid is "already stopped". Under `detached:yes`, the group kill stays keyed on the verified leader.
- [ ] **Port side:** after the kill, a port holder is the server's survivor only when it matches the recorded listener identity, or (under `detached:yes`) its process group is the recorded leader's. Any other holder is reported as "port {port} held by unrelated pid {x}", and the record is deleted, since the recorded server is gone.
- [ ] **One executable helper:** add a `plugin/bin/` CLI (e.g. `dev-server.js` with `record` and `stop` verbs, using the injectable-runner seam in `.claude/skills/gh-api-module-pattern`'s CLI wrapper contract). Every prose site above calls it instead of restating the stop: the Ephemeral server start's item 4 (record), Section D, `step3-routing.md`, the standalone stop, and both `/flow` multi-spec teardown sites (stop).
- [ ] **Legacy records:** a run whose record has no sidecar (started before this change) keeps today's behavior, logged once as `identity unverified (legacy record)`. Give that branch a removal condition per this repo's deprecation rule.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Unit tests with a fake process table: a recorded pid whose start time differs is not signalled and reports already stopped; a matching one is signalled; a port held by the recorded listener (alive after a leader-only stop) is reported as the survivor and the record is kept; a port held by an unrelated process is reported as unrelated and the record is deleted; a `detached:yes` child in the leader's process group counts as the survivor
- Each of those tests goes red against a helper that skips the identity check
- A conformance test asserts that none of the stop sites restate `kill {pid}` / `taskkill /PID` / an `lsof … | xargs kill` stop inline and that each one calls the helper
- A live probe on macOS (and Linux in CI where available) starts a real `setsid` shell-leader server, records it, and stops it through the helper, with the leader and listener identities matching what `ps` reports
- `npm test` passes

## Release Note

Pipeline cleanup no longer signals a process that merely reused a dead dev server's pid, and no longer blames an unrelated process for a port it failed to free.

## Technical Approach

The two candidate rules in the original question were a pid-listens-on-port probe (it fails for the shell-leader/child shape, as the record notes) and some stronger identity. Start time is the standard way to tell a reused pid from the original. POSIX: `ps -o lstart= -p {pid}` or `ps -o etimes=`; win32: `Win32_Process.CreationDate` via PowerShell `Get-CimInstance`. A reused pid cannot share its predecessor's start time. Capturing the listener's own identity at start, instead of deriving it from the leader at stop, sidesteps the reparenting problem entirely.

Listener lookup at record time: POSIX `lsof -nP -iTCP:{port} -sTCP:LISTEN -t`, with `ss -ltnp` as a fallback where `lsof` is absent; win32 `Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort {port} -State Listen` → `OwningProcess`.

Fail direction: an identity the helper cannot read (no `ps`, a CIM failure) is unprovable, so it signals nothing and reports a cleanup failure, keeping the record. A leaked dev server is recoverable; a killed unrelated process is not.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/dev-server.js` — new CLI: `record` and `stop` verbs
- `plugin/bin/lib/dev-server/` — new module: identity capture, verify, stop (injectable runner)
- `plugin/skills/_shared/dev-url-detection.md` — Ephemeral server start item 4 (record via helper), standalone stop
- `plugin/skills/wrap-up/cleanup-procedures-execution.md` — Section D steps 2-4 call the helper
- `plugin/skills/review/step3-routing.md` — fix-wave server coordination
- `plugin/skills/flow/multispec-review-console.md` — shared teardown step 1
- `plugin/skills/flow/multispec-parallel-waves.md` — per-member server stop
- `tests/bin-lib/dev-server/` — unit tests with a fake process table
- `docs/plugin-structure.md` — list the new CLI and module

## Gotchas

- ASSUMPTION — verify at build: `ps -o lstart=` and `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` return a start time stable enough to compare exactly (second resolution) on the CI runners; if `etimes` is used instead, compare with a small tolerance and test the boundary.
- ASSUMPTION — verify at build: once the readiness poll succeeds, the listener is already bound and visible to `lsof`/`ss`/`Get-NetTCPConnection` without elevated privileges on macOS, Linux CI, and win32 CI. The original record noted no probe had been run against a real `detached:no` / `detached:yes` leader — run one before relying on it.
- The `bin/` CLIs must not read `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` at runtime (unset in Bash); follow the existing CLIs' process-cwd anchoring.
- `multispec-parallel-waves.md`'s members may start servers without a run-dir sidecar path; check where each member writes its record before wiring the helper.

## Original request
